entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: Rogue server can drive large heap allocations from server-declared lengths in OK packets
entry.content:
Summary

MariaDB Connector/J sized heap allocations from lengths declared by the server in OK packets before checking that those lengths fit in the packet. A rogue or MitM server can make the client allocate megabytes from a packet of a few bytes.

Details

When CLIENT_SESSION_TRACK is negotiated (the default), an OK packet carries an info field followed by session-state blocks, each tracked variable being sent as a length-encoded name and value. OkPacket.parse() and parseWithInfo() allocated new byte[len] for the info field, the variable name and the value with the server-declared len, then copied the packet data into it. The copy failed with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the packet was shorter, but only after the allocation had taken place.

A server-declared length of 8 MiB in an 18-byte packet was enough to trigger an 8 MiB allocation; the integer-range validation of length-encoded values does not help, since such lengths are valid positive integers.

The fix validates every server-declared length against the remaining packet bytes before any allocation (ReadableByteBuf.checkLength() and a bounded readBytes(int)), and stops reading the session state at the first inconsistent entry.

Impact

Availability only: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can drive attacker-controlled heap allocations on every OK packet, creating GC pressure up to OutOfMemoryError in the client application. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection; no authentication bypass, confidentiality or integrity impact.

Credit

Reported by fg0x0

entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: Length-encoded integers larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE were truncated before being used as lengths
entry.content:
Summary

MariaDB Connector/J narrowed 8-byte length-encoded integers received from the server to int without validation. A rogue or MitM server can send a value above Integer.MAX_VALUE whose truncation becomes a negative or arbitrary length.

Details

The protocol encodes lengths as length-encoded integers, whose 8-byte form the decoder (readLength() and readIntLengthEncodedNotNull()) returned as (int) readLong(). A value above Integer.MAX_VALUE therefore wrapped to a negative or unrelated int, used afterwards as a length to size allocations or reads, which ended in NegativeArraySizeException, out-of-bounds exceptions or oversized allocations.

The fix rejects any length-encoded value that does not fit a non-negative int with an explicit error.

Impact

Availability only: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can crash the client's connection handling with unchecked exceptions or drive oversized allocations. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection; no authentication bypass, confidentiality or integrity impact.

Credit

Reported by fg0x0

entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: XA recover() trusted server-supplied gtrid and bqual lengths
entry.content:
Summary

XAResource.recover() in MariaDB Connector/J trusted the gtrid_length and bqual_length columns returned by XA RECOVER to allocate and split each Xid.

Details

MariaDbPoolConnection and MariaDbPoolPinnedConnection built each Xid of the recovery list by allocating new byte[gtrid_length] and new byte[bqual_length] and copying from the data column, without validating the lengths against the XA specification bounds (Xid.MAXGTRIDSIZE, Xid.MAXBQUALSIZE) or the actual payload. Negative or oversized lengths, or lengths that do not fit the data, ended in large allocations or unchecked exceptions (NegativeArraySizeException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) during recovery.

The fix validates the lengths before any allocation or copy and reports an invalid row as an XAException (XAER_RMFAIL).

Impact

Availability only, and limited to applications running XA recovery: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can crash the recovery or drive large allocations. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection.

Credit

Reported by fg0x0

entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file check could be satisfied by text inside quoted identifiers, letting a malicious server read client files
entry.content:
Summary

MariaDB Connector/J checked a server's LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file request by searching the text of the command it had sent for LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '<file>'. The search also matched inside quoted identifiers, string literals and comments, so text returned by the server and re-used in a later query could satisfy it. A rogue or MitM server can read any file the client JVM can read.

Details

When a server answers a command with a LOCAL INFILE request (0xFB packet), the connector opens the named file on the client host and streams it to the server, after verifying that the file corresponds to a LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE of the command it sent (ClientMessage.validateLocalFileName()). That verification was a regular expression whose prefix accepted any character, so it answered "does the text appear anywhere in the SQL", including inside a backtick-quoted identifier.

Several driver paths put identifiers returned by the server straight back into their next query: DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys() and getExportedKeys() re-use database and table names from SHOW DATABASES, SHOW TABLES and the REFERENCES clause of SHOW CREATE TABLE output, and updatable result sets build their UPDATE and refresh SELECT from the schema and table names of the column definition packets. A server returning an identifier such as LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd' makes the connector send SHOW CREATE TABLE `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd'`.`accounts` ; the server answers it with a LOCAL INFILE request for /etc/passwd, the check passes, and the file content is sent. On the getImportedKeys() path the resulting error is swallowed and the application observes nothing. The same applies to an application that interpolates identifiers obtained from the server into its own queries.

The fix parses the command instead of searching it: string literals, quoted identifiers and comments are skipped, statements are split on ;, and only a LOAD DATA|XML [LOW_PRIORITY|CONCURRENT] LOCAL INFILE found at the start of a statement is considered, its file literal or bound parameter being compared exactly to the requested file.

Impact

Confidentiality: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can read arbitrary files from the host running the JDBC client (application configuration, credential files, key stores, ...) through standard java.sql calls such as DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys(), getExportedKeys() or ResultSet.updateRow(). Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection and allowLocalInfile enabled (the default). Setting allowLocalInfile=false is a workaround when LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE is not needed. No integrity or availability impact.

Credit

Reported by buxuwa (buxu) through HackerOne

entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file check could be satisfied by text inside quoted identifiers, letting a malicious server read client files
entry.content:
Summary

MariaDB Connector/J checked a server's LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file request by searching the text of the command it had sent for LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '<file>'. The search also matched inside quoted identifiers, string literals and comments, so text returned by the server and re-used in a later query could satisfy it. A rogue or MitM server can read any file the client JVM can read.

Details

When a server answers a command with a LOCAL INFILE request (0xFB packet), the connector opens the named file on the client host and streams it to the server, after verifying that the file corresponds to a LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE of the command it sent (ClientMessage.validateLocalFileName()). That verification was a regular expression whose prefix accepted any character, so it answered "does the text appear anywhere in the SQL", including inside a backtick-quoted identifier.

Several driver paths put identifiers returned by the server straight back into their next query: DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys() and getExportedKeys() re-use database and table names from SHOW DATABASES, SHOW TABLES and the REFERENCES clause of SHOW CREATE TABLE output, and updatable result sets build their UPDATE and refresh SELECT from the schema and table names of the column definition packets. A server returning an identifier such as LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd' makes the connector send SHOW CREATE TABLE `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd'`.`accounts` ; the server answers it with a LOCAL INFILE request for /etc/passwd, the check passes, and the file content is sent. On the getImportedKeys() path the resulting error is swallowed and the application observes nothing. The same applies to an application that interpolates identifiers obtained from the server into its own queries.

The fix parses the command instead of searching it: string literals, quoted identifiers and comments are skipped, statements are split on ;, and only a LOAD DATA|XML [LOW_PRIORITY|CONCURRENT] LOCAL INFILE found at the start of a statement is considered, its file literal or bound parameter being compared exactly to the requested file.

Impact

Confidentiality: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can read arbitrary files from the host running the JDBC client (application configuration, credential files, key stores, ...) through standard java.sql calls such as DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys(), getExportedKeys() or ResultSet.updateRow(). Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection and allowLocalInfile enabled (the default). Setting allowLocalInfile=false is a workaround when LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE is not needed. No integrity or availability impact.

Credit

Reported by buxuwa (buxu) through HackerOne

entry.title: [org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client] MariaDB Connector/J: Server could switch character_set_results away from UTF-8 without the client noticing
entry.content:
Summary

MariaDB Connector/J decodes every result as UTF-8 and guards character_set_client against a change to another charset, but did not guard character_set_results, and relied on the server's global session_track_system_variables list to be told about charset changes at all.

Details

The connector learns about session variable changes through session tracking, and closes the connection when character_set_client is switched away from UTF-8, so that its UTF-8 decoding stays correct. Two gaps remained:

  • character_set_results was not guarded: a server could switch it to another charset, after which the bytes of every result were decoded as UTF-8 although encoded otherwise.
  • the list of tracked variables came from the server's global session_track_system_variables: a server configured, or made, not to track the character set variables could change them silently.

The fix requests an explicit session tracking list that includes both character set variables whatever the server's global setting, and closes the connection when character_set_results is changed to a charset other than utf8, utf8mb3 or utf8mb4, as it already did for character_set_client.

Impact

Integrity: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can make the strings an application reads differ from the bytes the server returned (inappropriate encoding for the output context), which can defeat application-side validation or escaping built on those values. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection; no confidentiality or availability impact.

Credit

Reported by fg0x0

entry.title: [gov.nsa.emissary:emissary] NationalSecurityAgency/emissary has an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-35571
entry.content:
Summary

The URL validation regex ^(https?:/)?/.* added to emissary's NavAction.java allows protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com/...) and single-slash scheme variants (http:/evil.com) to bypass validation, enabling SSRF and open redirect attacks.

Affected Package

  • Ecosystem: Maven
  • Package: NationalSecurityAgency/emissary
  • Affected versions: < e2078417464b
  • Patched versions: >= e2078417464b

Severity

Medium

CWE

CWE-918 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

Details

The fix in NavAction.java (line 47) introduces a VALID_LINK pattern:

Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")

This regex is intended to restrict navigation links to relative paths and HTTP/HTTPS URLs. However, it has multiple bypass vectors.

Protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com/...): The group (https?:/)? is optional, so the pattern reduces to //.* when the group is absent. This matches //evil.com/steal?c=SESSION, which browsers resolve to the current page's protocol plus the attacker's host.

Single-slash scheme (http:/evil.com): The regex group captures http:/ as a valid match, and browsers normalize http:/evil.com to http://evil.com, creating an open redirect to the attacker's server.

Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (//169.254.169.254/...): This enables SSRF to cloud instance metadata endpoints, which is particularly dangerous in AWS/GCP environments where IAM credentials can be retrieved.

The pre-fix code had no validation at all, accepting any URL. The fix blocks javascript:, ftp:, and data: URIs, but the protocol-relative and single-slash bypasses remain exploitable.

PoC

"""
CVE-2026-35571 - NationalSecurityAgency/emissary SSRF via NavAction

The fix in commit e2078417464b adds URL scheme validation using:
    Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")

This allows protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com) and single-slash variants
(http:/evil.com) to bypass the validation.

Tested against: emissary@0d4dc56 (pre-fix) and patch e207841
Extracted from: src/main/java/emissary/server/mvc/NavAction.java:47
"""

import re
import sys

FIXED_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^(https?:/)?/.*")


def vulnerable_accepts(link: str) -> bool:
    """Pre-fix behaviour: no validation, everything passes."""
    return True


def fixed_accepts(link: str) -> bool:
    """Post-fix behaviour: must match VALID_LINK pattern."""
    return bool(FIXED_PATTERN.match(link))


TEST_VECTORS = [
    ("javascript: XSS payload",
     "javascript:alert(document.cookie)", True),
    ("ftp: scheme",
     "ftp://evil.com/exfil", True),
    ("data: URI",
     "data:text/html,<script>alert(1)</script>", True),

    ("Relative path",
     "/path/to/resource", False),
    ("HTTP URL",
     "http://trusted.internal:8080/api", False),
    ("HTTPS URL",
     "https://trusted.internal/api", False),

    ("Protocol-relative URL to attacker host (//evil.com)",
     "//evil.com/steal?c=SESSION", True),
    ("Protocol-relative with embedded credentials",
     "//user:pass@evil.com/path", True),
    ("Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (//169.254.169.254)",
     "//169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/", True),
    ("Backslash trick (\\\\evil.com)",
     "\\\\evil.com/path", True),
    ("Tab in scheme (java\\tscript:...)",
     "java\tscript:alert(1)", True),
    ("Path starting with attacker-like host (/evil.com)",
     "/evil.com", False),
    ("Triple slash (///evil.com)",
     "///evil.com/etc/passwd", True),
    ("http:/ single-slash to attacker host",
     "http:/evil.com/steal", True),
    ("https:/ single-slash to attacker host",
     "https:/evil.com/steal", True),
    ("URL-encoded javascript scheme (%6a...)",
     "%6aavascript:alert(1)", True),
    ("CRLF injection in path",
     "/legit\r\nLocation: http://evil.com", True),
]


def main():
    print("=" * 72)
    print("CVE-2026-35571 -- Emissary NavAction SSRF / Open-Redirect PoC")
    print("Pattern under test: ^(https?:/)?/.*")
    print("=" * 72)
    print()

    bypasses_found = []
    results_table = []

    for desc, url, should_block in TEST_VECTORS:
        vuln_result = vulnerable_accepts(url)
        fixed_result = fixed_accepts(url)

        if should_block and fixed_result:
            status = "BYPASS"
            bypasses_found.append((desc, url))
        elif should_block and not fixed_result:
            status = "BLOCKED (good)"
        elif not should_block and fixed_result:
            status = "ALLOWED (good)"
        elif not should_block and not fixed_result:
            status = "FALSE-POS"
        else:
            status = "UNKNOWN"

        results_table.append((desc, url, vuln_result, fixed_result, status))

    for desc, url, vuln, fixed, status in results_table:
        display_url = repr(url) if len(url) > 50 else url
        print(f"[{status:>15}]  {desc}")
        print(f"{'':>17}  URL: {display_url}")
        print(f"{'':>17}  pre-fix={vuln}  post-fix={fixed}")
        print()

    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"Total vectors tested : {len(TEST_VECTORS)}")
    print(f"Bypasses found       : {len(bypasses_found)}")
    print()

    if bypasses_found:
        print("VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED -- the following vectors bypass the fix:")
        print()
        for desc, url in bypasses_found:
            print(f"  - {desc}")
            print(f"    URL: {repr(url)}")
        print()
        print("Key finding: The regex ^(https?:/)?/.* allows protocol-relative")
        print("URLs (//evil.com/...) because the optional group (https?:/) can be")
        print("absent, leaving //.* which matches //attacker.com. This enables")
        print("SSRF to arbitrary external hosts via navigation links.")
        print()
        print("Additionally, http:/evil.com and https:/evil.com match the regex")
        print("(group 1 captures 'http:/' or 'https:/') and browsers normalise")
        print("these to http://evil.com, enabling open redirect / SSRF.")
        sys.exit(0)
    else:
        print("No bypasses found -- fix appears complete.")
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Run python3 poc.py
  2. Observe that protocol-relative and single-slash URLs bypass the regex

Expected output:

VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED
Protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com/) and single-slash variants (http:/evil.com) bypass the regex validation.

Impact

An attacker can craft navigation links that bypass URL validation to redirect users to attacker-controlled servers (open redirect) or make the emissary server issue requests to internal services (SSRF). The //169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ bypass is particularly dangerous in cloud environments, enabling retrieval of IAM credentials.

Suggested Remediation

Replace the regex with one that explicitly rejects protocol-relative URLs. Alternatively, parse the URL with java.net.URI and validate the scheme and host against an allowlist rather than relying on regex.

References

  • Incomplete fix commit: https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/commit/e2078417464b9004620dde28dcbca2f73ea06c13
  • Original CVE: CVE-2026-35571

References

  • https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/security/advisories/GHSA-c6q7-wqw2-h65w
  • https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/security/advisories/GHSA-cpm7-cfpx-3hvp
  • https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/commit/e2078417464b9004620dde28dcbca2f73ea06c13

entry.title: [org.keycloak:keycloak-services] Keycloak vulnerable to cross-site scripting (xss) via case-insensitive uri validation bypass
entry.content:
Description

A flaw was found in Keycloak. A remote attacker with administrative privileges, specifically those with manage-client permission or access to client registration endpoints, could bypass client Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) validation. This is achieved by registering a malicious client with a specially crafted redirect URI using a case-insensitive javascript: or data: scheme. This Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability allows for arbitrary code execution in the Keycloak origin when a victim clicks the crafted link, such as in the logout flow or the Admin Console.

entry.title: [org.keycloak:keycloak-services] Keycloak vulnerable to information disclosure through arbitrary filesystem path probing
entry.content:
Description

A flaw was found in Keycloak. A realm administrator with the "manage-realm" role can exploit this vulnerability by submitting an arbitrary filesystem path as a keystore parameter when creating a key provider component. This allows the administrator to probe arbitrary filesystem paths, determining which files exist and are readable by the Keycloak process. This information disclosure could be used to identify high-value targets for follow-on attacks.
